title: Literary Analysis and Critical Theory
learningObjectives: Master sophisticated vocabulary for literary analysis and critical theory
Understand major literary movements, genres, and analytical frameworks
Practice close reading and interpretation of complex literary texts
Recognize terminology used in literary criticism and cultural studies

sections.title: The Art of Literary Interpretation
sections.content:
Literary analysis represents one of the most sophisticated forms of textual engagement — demanding deep interpretation, aesthetic appreciation, and critical evaluation. Literature operates on multiple levels simultaneously: narrative, symbolic, formal, historical, and ideological.

This lesson explores vocabulary and frameworks for advanced literary analysis, from close reading to critical theories, from genre conventions to rhetorical devices. Mastering this discourse enables articulation of sophisticated interpretations and participation in conversations about meaning, aesthetics, and the human condition.

sections.title: Narrative Structure and Literary Devices
sections.content:
<Narrative> encompasses story and discourse. <In medias res> begins mid-action. Flashback (analepsis) and foreshadowing (prolepsis) manipulate time. <Third-person limited> accesses one consciousness; <third-person omniscient> knows all. <Unreliable narrator> creates ambiguity.

<Stream of consciousness> mimics thought. <Round characters> are complex; <flat characters> one-dimensional. Symbolism invests objects with meaning beyond the literal.

Irony involves discrepancy — verbal, situational, or dramatic. <Allusion> references other texts. <Heteroglossia> describes coexisting voices within a text. <Verisimilitude> — the appearance of truth — distinguishes compelling fiction.

sections.title: Critical Approaches and Theoretical Frameworks
sections.content:
Formalism or <New Criticism> focuses on text itself — structure, language, devices — bracketing intent and context. Post-structuralism (Derrida) destabilizes meaning, revealing aporias.

<Psychoanalytic criticism> explores unconscious desires. <Marxist criticism> examines class and ideology. <Feminist criticism> analyzes gender and patriarchal structures.

<Postcolonial theory> investigates colonialism's legacy. <Queer theory> interrogates heteronormativity. <New Historicism> views literature and history as mutually constitutive. <Ecocriticism> examines nature representation. Sophisticated analysis integrates multiple frameworks.

sections.title: Genre, Form, and Literary Movements
sections.content:
Genre categorizes literature by form: novel, <short story>, poetry, drama. Subgenres include bildungsroman (coming-of-age), <epistolary novel> (letters), picaresque, gothic. Poetry employs meter, <rhyme scheme>, stanza structure. <Free verse> lacks regular meter. <Enjambment> continues sentences across lines.

<Romanticism> emphasized emotion, nature, individualism. Realism depicted ordinary life. <Modernism> experimented with form, fragmentation, subjectivity. <Postmodernism> embraces metafiction, pastiche, intertextuality, and skepticism toward grand narratives.

Understanding genre conventions and historical contexts enriches interpretation.

sections.title: Literary Critical Discourse
sections.content:
Example 1: CLOSE READING - <The recurring water imagery functions as complex symbol of purification and dissolution, mirroring psychological fragmentation.>

Example 2: THEORETICAL - <A Foucauldian reading reveals how disciplinary mechanisms constitute subjectivity through internalization of regulatory norms.>

Example 3: INTERTEXTUAL - <The text's palimpsestic quality demands recognition of its dialogic relationship with precursors, enacting Bloom's "anxiety of influence."> <Ekphrasis> creates dialogue between verbal and visual representation.

sections.title: Postcolonial Literature and Contemporary Voices
sections.content:
<Postcolonial literary theory> examines literature produced after colonialism — how power structures persist and how colonized peoples reclaim narrative agency.

• <Writing back> — rewriting canonical texts from the colonized perspective (e.g., Rhys's "Wide Sargasso Sea")
• <Hybridity> — Bhabha's concept of cultural mixing in the <third space>
• <Subaltern> — Spivak's term for groups excluded from dominant discourse
• <Magical realism> — supernatural elements representing experiences resisting Western rationalism

Contemporary literature reflects <transnational> identities, <multilingual> consciousness, and <diaspora>.

sections.title: Literary Critical Analysis
sections.content:
Example 1: POSTCOLONIAL - <Achebe's "Things Fall Apart" performs cultural reclamation by demonstrating pre-colonial Igbo society's complex values and aesthetics — refuting colonial primitivism narratives.>

Example 2: NARRATIVE - <Morrison's fragmented structure in "Beloved" embodies traumatic memory — the past erupting unbidden, resisting chronological containment.>

Example 3: INTERTEXTUAL - <Stoppard's "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern" inhabits canonical text from the margins, transforming minor characters into existential protagonists.>

sections.title: Literary Mastery
sections.content:
Literary analysis at its highest synthesizes textual attention with theoretical sophistication. Great readers balance interpretive possibilities, recognize ambiguity as richness, and understand meaning is actively constructed through interpretation.

Literary criticism at its best is creative intellectual work — engaging in conversations about literature's significance. The frameworks here provide tools for this engagement.

keyVocabulary.definition: An irresolvable internal contradiction or logical impasse in a text
keyVocabulary.example: Deconstructive reading reveals the aporia at the heart of the text's argument.

keyVocabulary.definition: A text bearing traces of earlier, erased writing; layered meanings
keyVocabulary.example: The novel functions as a palimpsest, with earlier narratives visible beneath the surface.

keyVocabulary.definition: The presence of multiple voices or discourses within a text
keyVocabulary.example: Bakhtin's concept of heteroglossia captures the novel's polyphonic nature.

keyVocabulary.definition: Groups marginalized and excluded from hegemonic power structures
keyVocabulary.example: Postcolonial theory asks whether the subaltern can speak within dominant discourse.

keyVocabulary.definition: The appearance of being true or real; lifelikeness
keyVocabulary.example: Realist fiction strives for verisimilitude in depicting everyday life.

keyVocabulary.definition: Vivid literary description of a visual work of art
keyVocabulary.example: The poem's ekphrastic passage brings the painting to life through language.
